name: Christina Larner
specialization: Scottish witch-hunting; state formation; gender and prosecution; Calvinist religious culture

major_works.title: Enemies of God: The Witch-Hunt in Scotland
major_works.significance: Foundational study of Scottish witch-hunting integrating state formation theory with gender analysis; argued prosecution was both religiously driven and politically functional

major_works.title: Witchcraft and Religion: The Politics of Popular Belief
major_works.significance: Posthumous collection of essays on the politics of witchcraft belief; influential despite Larner's early death

core_argument: Scottish witch-hunting was driven by Calvinist state formation: the post-Reformation Scottish state, led by Kirk and crown, used witch prosecution as a mechanism for imposing godly discipline on the population. While witch-hunting was 'woman-hunting' in the sense that women were disproportionately targeted, this was not the exclusive or primary motivation; state religious ideology was the driving force.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Scottish privy council records, circuit court records, presbytery records from 1560-1727; state and church administrative documents
methodological_approach.analysis_target: State-church institutional dynamics; gender demographics of accused; relationship between persecution intensity and political/religious crisis
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Institutional analysis combined with quantitative prosecution data; sociological state-formation theory applied to historical record
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: State-formation and religious ideology: macro-political structure driving persecution

key_contributions.claim: The Scottish witch-hunt intensified during periods of Calvinist state-building; prosecution served the project of creating a godly commonwealth under Kirk discipline
key_contributions.implication: Witch-hunting should be analyzed as a state-building tool, not only as popular superstition or community-level conflict

key_contributions.claim: Witch-hunting was disproportionately directed at women but was not solely or primarily about gender; religious and political factors were equally important
key_contributions.implication: Gender cannot be the sole explanatory variable; it operated within a matrix of religious and state power

key_contributions.claim: The specifically Calvinist theology of Scottish Protestantism — its emphasis on devil's power, moral discipline, and godly polity — created uniquely intense conditions for witch-hunting
key_contributions.implication: Denominational differences in Protestant theology produced different prosecution intensities

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Sociology of religion (Weber on Calvinist discipline), state formation theory, feminist historiography
criticisms: Died at 49 before completing a projected comprehensive study
Some feminist historians felt her qualification of the 'woman-hunting' thesis was an understatement of gender's role
Scottish focus limits generalizability, though she explicitly contextualized Scotland comparatively

historiographical_significance: Larner's work gave Scottish witchcraft historiography its foundational framework and introduced state-formation theory to the field. Her contribution to feminist analysis — acknowledging gender while insisting on multi-causality — influenced subsequent gender historians including Roper. Her early death left a gap in Scottish witchcraft scholarship that Goodare's Survey of Scottish Witchcraft later partially addressed.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
